claims.claim: Critics stress that Tolkien's impression of depth and historical background is what formulaic followers fail to replicate.

Le Guin characterised Tolkien's prose as quieter English of simple timelessness with sobriety, wit and force, ranging easily from the commonplace to the stately and able to slide into metrical poetry.

Tolkien defended Théoden's archaic speech on the ground that modern dialogue would create an insincerity of thought and a disunion of word and meaning, and gave Elrond the most archaisms as the eldest speaker.
claims.quote: a disunion of word and meaning

claims.claim: Le Guin faulted Zelazny and Leiber for talking colloquial American English when humour is intended and reverting to old formal usages at earnest moments.
claims.source: The Language of the Night by Ursula K Le Guin (Murray Ewing)
claims.quote: at earnest moments they revert to old formal usages

claims.claim: Le Guin's test is to change a passage's names to mundane ones and see whether it still reads as fantasy; Kurtz's Deryni fails as fancy dress.
claims.source: The Language of the Night by Ursula K Le Guin (Murray Ewing)

claims.claim: Le Guin warned against forced archaic language as a crutch, praising Tolkien's plain clear English, concrete vocabulary that avoids 'ichor', and the principle that the style is the book.
claims.source: From Elfland to Poughkeepsie to The Witcher (Nick Gibney)

claims.claim: Applying Le Guin, TheOneRing.net found The Rings of Power's 'Okay', 'like', 'Nah', 'Yeah' and 'conflicted' expose modern minds, while its over-correction lapses into fortune-cookie 'High Aphorism'.
claims.source: From The Rings of Power to Poughkeepsie (TheOneRing.net, 2022)

claims.claim: Le Guin's essay separates the risky inner lands of Elfland from banal imitation that is the outside world in disguise, and Beagle called it the definitive piece on fantasy.
Brennan observes writers sticking '-st' on every second-person verb and '-th' on every third-person one, and warns archaic grammar is very easily overused.
Epic fantasy's archaisms fall into be-perfects ('Winter is come'), be- prefixes, hither/thither, thou/thee, postposed modifiers and do-less imperatives, used to suggest a whole past speech community.
claims.source: The 'Ye Olde' in Epic Fantasy: 6 More Archaisms (Thoughts on Fantasy)

claims.claim: A commenter notes the Nazgûl uses thee/thou while Éowyn answers in modern 'you', and that Tolkien was very deliberate about when he used 'thou'.
claims.source: The 'Ye Olde' in Epic Fantasy: 6 More Archaisms (Thoughts on Fantasy)
claims.quote: very deliberate about when he used 'thou'

claims.claim: 'From whence it came' is a common archaism error because 'whence' already contains 'from'.
claims.source: The 'Ye Olde' in Epic Fantasy: 6 More Archaisms (Thoughts on Fantasy)

claims.claim: Bored of the Rings steps through the prologue, the map and the main text in turn, substituting brand names (Moxie and Pepsi, Serutan) for Tolkien's invented terms.
The parody replaces Tolkien's Sindarin hymn with nonsense modern references ('Unicef clearasil') and parodies the Watcher in the Water as a thesaurus-monster.
David Bratman remarked that the parodists wrought better than they knew, since Tolkien's drafts came close to writing the parody version of his own novel before he avoided it.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that critics stress formulaic followers fail to replicate that depth/historical background
verdicts.trueWording: an impression of depth behind the action
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200) has 'an impression of depth' three times verbatim, plus 'an extensive history behind the action'. But the page never links depth to what imitators fail at: its imitation critique is Attebery on The Sword of Shannara, 'to evoke wonder without engaging the mind or emotions', reducing Tolkien's artistry 'to a bare formula', and Kincaid on 'multi-volume Tolkien clones'. No critic on the page is quoted saying depth/historical background is the unreplicated element.

verdicts.trueWording: quieter... simple timelessness... sobriety, wit and force
verdicts.note: Blogspot post quotes Le Guin: 'quieter and [with] a less extraordinary English, or rather an English extraordinary for its simple timelessness... It has sobriety, wit and force... It ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately, and can slide into metrical poetry'. Quote 'sobriety, wit and force' verbatim; every limb (timelessness, sobriety/wit/force, commonplace-to-stately range, metrical poetry) on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: an insincerity of thought, a disunion of word and meaning
verdicts.note: Page: 'Responding to criticism of Theoden's dialogue in "The Golden Hall", Tolkien claims that to utilize a modern style would result in, "an insincerity of thought, a disunion of word and meaning."' and 'Elrond, the oldest of the council has lived since the First Age, and speaks with the most archaisms as a result of this' (attributed there to Shippey's analysis). Both limbs verbatim-supported.

verdicts.trueWording: When humour is intended the characters talk colloquial American English
verdicts.note: Murray Ewing page: 'says Leiber and Zelazny could do better ("When humour is intended the characters talk colloquial American English, or even slang, and at earnest moments they revert to old formal usages.")'. Quote verbatim; both limbs and both authors named.

verdicts.trueWording: change the names... see if it still reads as fantasy
verdicts.note: Page: 'The test is simple: take any passage, change the names from mock-fantasy ones to mundane ones, and see if it still reads as fantasy. She uses as an example a passage from Katherine Kurtz's Deryni series... it's not fantasy, it's fancy dress.' Quote 'fancy dress' verbatim. Minor nuance recorded, not a limb failure: the 'fancy dress' verdict is the blogger's own phrase about Le Guin's example, and the claim does not attribute it to Le Guin.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that Le Guin warned against forced archaic language 'as a crutch'
verdicts.trueWording: the tightrope of archaic language that Le Guin warns against
verdicts.note: Substack page (HTTP 200, raw HTML stripped) quotes Le Guin verbatim: 'Tolkien writes a plain, clear English... he has no "ichor"; everything is direct, concrete, and simple' and 'The style, of course, is the book.' Quote 'ichor' verbatim. The archaism limb is only partly there: the page says Sapkowski and Tolkien 'neither force themselves to walk the tightrope of archaic language that Le Guin warns against'. Nothing on the page calls archaism a crutch or gives that motive; 'crutch' does not occur on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: these Elves too frequently lapse into High Aphorism
verdicts.note: TheOneRing.net (26 Sep 2022) lists verbatim: hobbits who say 'Okay,' 'It means, like, what we do'; Numenoreans who say 'Nah'; Elves who say 'conflicted'; Dwarves who say 'Yeah'. 'Instead, however, these Elves too frequently lapse into High Aphorism' and 'we get fortune-cookie philosophy'. The modern-mind limb is the article's own argument ('a disunity of language and character. The spell has broken'; a king in modern idiom would not think 'Thus shall I sleep better'), and the over-correction limb is 'Overcompensating for modernism is, of course, an equally dangerous trap.'

verdicts.trueWording: genuine, risky Inner Lands... banal imitation... outside world in disguise
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: 'she distinguishes "the genuine, risky Inner Lands (Elfland) from the banal imitation which is really the outside world in disguise (Poughkeepsie)"' and 'The novelist Peter S. Beagle called it "the definitive piece on fantasy..."'. Quote verbatim; both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: stick '-st' on the end of every second-person verb
verdicts.note: Swan Tower page (c 2026 Marie Brennan, footer): 'Some writers seem unable to resist the urge to stick "-st" on the end of every second-person verb and "-th" on the end of every third-person one, no matter what it is.' and 'But archaic grammar is something that is very easily overused.' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that these six categories are the set epic fantasy's archaisms 'fall into'
verdicts.trueWording: a whole past speech community with a different social hierarchy
verdicts.note: All six categories are on the page as numbered items 6-11: 6 'Winter is Come' (be for have), 7 the be- prefix, 8 hither/thither adverbials, 9 thou & thee, 10 repositioning modifiers, 11 imperatives/questions (stated subject, omitted 'do'). Purpose limb verbatim: 'to suggest not just the past, but a whole past speech community'. But the post frames these as 'the remaining 6' of an eleven-item list continued from the previous week (which covered 'here be dragons', 'unsavoury louts they were', 'prithee'), so the six are not the whole taxonomy the claim implies.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that one commenter made both observations - they are two different commenters
verdicts.trueWording: Ksenia on Eowyn's 'you'; bdandmcfoster on Tolkien's deliberate 'thou'
verdicts.note: Both observations are in the comment thread, but by different people. Ksenia (21 Aug 2019): 'notice that Eowyn herself doesn't say "thee" or "thy", she just says "you."' bdandmcfoster (16 Sep 2020): 'Tolkien was very deliberate about when he used "thou" and when he used "you", and explains this in, I think, one of the appendices.' Quote is word-for-word (page uses curly double quotes around thou). The article body separately quotes the Nazgul's thee/thy speech to Eowyn.

Page quotes the Fellowship film line 'cast back into the fiery chasm from whence it came', then: 'this line uses "from" as well as "whence", which isn't really necessary as whence already incorporates "from"... this article suggests that not only is this wrong, but this is an error English speakers have been making for quite a long time.' Quote 'from whence' verbatim; reason limb explicit. Recorded nuance, not a limb failure: the author hedges ('I'd hesitate to proclaim this grammatically incorrect because I'm no expert') and sources the 'error' judgement to a linked article.

verdicts.trueWording: in turn mocking the prologue, the map, and the main text
verdicts.note: No quote field supplied, so graded on substance. Wikipedia: 'The parody steps through The Lord of the Rings, in turn mocking the prologue, the map, and the main text. The text combines slapstick humor with deliberately inappropriate use of brand names.' Brand-name limb: 'the carbonated beverages Moxie and Pepsi replace Merry and Pippin' and 'Saruman is satirised as Serutan, a laxative'. Every limb supported almost word for word.

verdicts.trueWording: A Unicef clearasil / Gibberish 'n' drivel... mocking the Sindarin hymn
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: 'An ancient lament of the Auld Elves runs "A Unicef clearasil / Gibberish n drivel ... Sing hey nonny nembutal", mocking the Sindarin hymn A Elbereth Gilthoniel.' and 'In a parody of the Fellowship's encounter with the Watcher in the Water, the chapter includes: "Aiyee!" shouted Legolam. "A Thesaurus!" "Maim!" roared the monster. "Mutilate, mangle, crush. See HARM."' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Those parodists wrought better than they knew
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: 'The Tolkien scholar David Bratman, writing in Mythlore, quotes an extended passage... commenting "Those parodists wrought better than they knew". He explains that Tolkien, in his many drafts, came very close to "inadvertently writing the parody version of his own novel", though in the end he managed to avoid that, in Bratman's view, remarkably completely.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported.
